papers.title: Effector-triggered stomatal immunity prevents leaf invasion by bacterial pathogens
papers.abstract: The phytopathogen Pseudomonas syringae must enter the leaf interior through natural openings such as stomata to cause disease. Plants restrict pathogen entry into the leaf through non–self-recognition–driven stomatal closure. P. syringae counters this stomatal immunity by deploying a range of toxins and effectors. Here, we show that stomatal immunity in Arabidopsis thaliana is reinforced upon recognition of the ubiquitous P. syringae type III effector AvrE1 by the resistance protein CAR1. CAR1 expression is enriched in guard cells, and its activation prolongs the effective duration of stomatal immunity. We also show that CAR1 prevents the invasion of leaf tissue by natural isolates of P. syringae , demonstrating that stomatal immunity provides a broadly significant barrier to host accessibility by P. syringae that carry the conserved effector AvrE1.
papers.affiliation: Department of Cell and Systems Biology, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 3G5, Canada.

papers.title: Medicinal plants, lessons from mushrooms and the power of smell: Books in brief
Pre-bilaterian roots of the chordate body plan
Strigolactone receptor D14 integrates phosphate and strigolactone signaling by interacting with and stabilizing PHR1
papers.abstract: Strigolactone (SL) and low phosphate (LP) signaling coordinately regulate shoot and root architecture and plant adaptation. While LP signaling is generally considered upstream of SL biosynthesis, their interaction is more complex. For instance, exogenous SL exerts opposite effects on lateral root formation under low versus high phosphorus. Here, we show that under LP, SL-induced anthocyanin accumulation requires PHR1, demonstrating that PHR1 functions downstream of SL signaling. We uncovered an SL-dependent physical interaction between PHR1 and the SL receptor DWARF14 (D14). This interaction promotes PHR1 dimerization, stabilizes PHR1 by inhibiting its ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and enhances its transcriptional activation activity. The D14-PHR1 complex directly binds and up-regulates the SL biosynthesis gene MAX3 and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes, thereby inhibiting branching and hypocotyl elongation and promoting anthocyanin accumulation. These findings indicate that PHR1 mediates the coordination of SL and LP signaling, potentially explaining SL’s opposing effects on lateral root formation under different phosphorus conditions. In the phr1 mutant, exogenous SL inhibited lateral roots under both LP and Pi-sufficient conditions, confirming that the promoting role of SL under LP requires PHR1. PHR1 also interacted with D14 to activate LBDs and HB23 , regulating lateral root formation. Collectively, LP signaling coordinates with SL signaling via two parallel pathways: regulating SL biosynthesis to align SL functions with LP requirements and enhancing PHR1 activity through PHR1-D14 interaction to amplify LP signaling outputs.

papers.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
papers.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

papers.title: Rapid activation kinetics of the NLR Swordholder underpin nonhost resistance to Phytophthora capsici in Nicotiana tabacum
papers.abstract: Nonhost resistance (NHR) represents a durable phenomenon where plants resist nonadapted pathogens. While NHR holds substantial potential for engineering crops with broad-spectrum and durable resistance, its underlying molecular mechanism remains incompletely understood. The oomycete pathogen Phytophthora capsici is nonadapted to Nicotiana tabacum (Nt) but is virulent on the closely related Nicotiana benthamiana (Nb). Here, we demonstrated that both species encode the NLR Swordholder (Swh), which recognizes P. capsici AvrNt effector proteins. NtSwh restores NHR in ntswh mutants, whereas NbSwh confers only partial resistance. Mechanistically, NtSwh exhibits weaker autoinhibition mediated by its amino-terminal extension domains, enabling rapid immune signaling that prevent pathogen effector–mediated suppression; NbSwh’s stronger autoinhibition delays activation, permitting effector suppression. Heterologous expression of NtSwh in tomato enhances field resistance to P. capsici without yield penalty. These findings indicate that the kinetics of NLR can play a key role in defining NHR, in addition to the presence or absence of specific NLRs, providing insights into strategies for breeding durable crop immunity.

papers.title: Precision recreation and multiplex stacking of disease-resistance alleles in tomato using optimized prime editing
papers.abstract: Abstract Prime editing enables precise modification of plant genomes and provides a means to recreate beneficial alleles underlying agronomically important traits. However, efficient and multiplexable prime editing systems remain limited in dicot crops. Here, we developed optimized prime editing systems for tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and applied them to engineer and stack disease-resistance alleles. Using three tomato prime editors, TomPE2, TomPE6c, and TomPE7, we recreated a naturally occurring resistance-associated deletion identified in pepper by precisely deleting two leucine residues from the CYSTM-domain proteins SlBs5 and SlBs5L. The resulting tomato lines exhibited enhanced resistance to Xanthomonas, demonstrating that a resistance allele can be functionally recreated across related crop species. In parallel, introduction of premature stop codons into the susceptibility gene SlDMR6 conferred resistance to both Xanthomonas and Pseudomonas syringae. Transcriptome profiling revealed distinct defense states: Slbs5/Slbs5L plants predominantly exhibited enhanced pathogen-induced defense responses, whereas Sldmr6 plants showed elevated basal defense. Comparison of prime editor architectures and culture temperatures revealed differences in editing activity and precision, with TomPE6c producing the highest proportion of precise edits. We further developed a modular multiplex prime editing system capable of simultaneously modifying multiple loci, enabling resistance alleles and regulatory variants to be combined within a single generation. The engineered alleles were stably inherited, and resistance phenotypes were maintained under elevated temperature conditions. Together, these results establish prime editing as an effective platform for precise recreation, engineering, and multiplex stacking of disease-resistance alleles and provide a framework for accelerating resistance breeding in crops.

papers.title: Telomere-to-telomere assemblies of Glycine soja and Glycine max uncover novel genomic features of soybean
papers.abstract: Abstract Achieving complete, gap-free genome assemblies remains a central challenge in genomics, particularly for repeat-rich plant genomes. Although several telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assemblies have been reported for soybean, highly repetitive genomic regions and the mitochondrial genome remain insufficiently resolved. Here, we assembled gap-free T2T nuclear genomes together with complete mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes for the wild soybean (Glycine soja) SoyW02 and the cultivated soybean (Glycine max) Zhonghuang 13. These assemblies substantially improved the resolution of repetitive genomic regions and enabled biological insights that were previously inaccessible. Comparative analyses uncovered a conserved subtelomeric exchange hub and refined the landscape of soybean satellite repeats, including pericentromere-enriched and chromosome-specific satellites. We further developed a de novo pipeline for identifying tandem duplication gene clusters, enabling systematic analyses of transcriptional and protein sequence divergence, and experimentally demonstrating expression and functional diversification between two duplicated oxidosqualene cyclases. Together, these assemblies establish a foundation for investigating the evolution and functional organization of repetitive genomic regions and will facilitate future soybean functional genomics and molecular breeding.

papers.title: Atypical phenylalanine ammonia-lyases that enhance phenylpropanoid production in plants
papers.abstract: Plants synthesize diverse phenylpropanoids, which provide us essential medicine, nutrients, and biomaterials while also acting as a major global carbon sink. Phenylpropanoids are primarily derived from L-phenylalanine (Phe) via Phe ammonia-lyase (PAL), a highly regulated enzymatic activity that limits phenylpropanoid production. However, it remains poorly understood how different plant species regulate PAL enzymes. Phylogeny-guided biochemical screening uncovered complex and diverse feedback regulation of PAL enzymes from 14 different plant species. This screening found a previously uncharacterized PAL clade, namely PALnc (from noncanonical), with some members exhibiting feedback activation by p -coumaric acid, caffeic acid, and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid in vitro. Transient expression of two PALnc genes, from Elaeis guineensis ( EgPALnc ) and Piper methysticum ( PmPALnc2 ), in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves elevated phenylpropanoid content, supported by the high in planta stability of PALnc proteins compared to canonical PALs. Whereas overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana PAL1 ( AtPAL1 ) in stable Arabidopsis transgenic lines resulted in very low accumulation of AtPAL1 protein and minor metabolic effects, introduction of EgPALnc rendered high content of EgPALnc protein and hyperaccumulation of hydroxycinnamates derivatives. Our findings uncover a previously overlooked diversity in the regulation of the entry step of phenylpropanoid biosynthesis across various plants and identify atypical PALs within the PALnc clade as valuable tools to debottleneck and enhance phenylpropanoid production in planta.
papers.affiliation: Department of Botany, University of Wisconsin-Madison

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomics reveals a novel variant of an energy signaling regulator for lateral branch domestication in cucumber
papers.abstract: Abstract Genetic alleles derived from wild resources are of great importance for crop breeding and improvement; however, connecting the dots between the functional variants and genetic traits is a significant challenge due to the need for precise, diverse, and large-scale phenotyping. Differential transcripts, which carry genetic variants or alternative splicing (AS) sites, may exhibit altered gene expression and protein coding, therefore influence phenotypes, showing their potential for high-throughput identification of functional genes. In this study, full-length transcripts were assembled and analyzed from eight developmental stage tissues of wild and cultivated cucumbers, utilizing PacBio Iso-seq and Illumina RNA-seq. We identified 6,980 genes underwent AS in cucumber. Approximately 66% of AS events were cultivar-specific, and genetic variants significantly increased around these divergent AS events. Based on the transcript structure of genes and variant annotation, we focused on cis-acting genetic variants that may affect gene function, in which a 21-bp insertion in the 5' untranslated region (UTR) of SnRK-Activating Kinase1 (CsSnAK1), an energy signaling regulator, was demonstrated to inhibit lateral branch development in cultivated cucumber by promoting CsSnAK1 mRNA abundance. Our work provides a straightforward yet reliable approach for integrating transcript structure and variant annotation to identify novel functional alleles in domestication traits.

papers.title: Distinct Splicing Complexes Formed by RS2Z32 Isoforms Modulate Alternative Splicing and Flowering
papers.abstract: Abstract Serine/arginine (SR) splicing factors can alter downstream precursor messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) splicing patterns and influence gene expression. However, the influences of different isoforms generated by alternative splicing of SR proteins themselves on the transcription and splicing of downstream target genes in plants remain to be elucidated. Here, we demonstrate that the interaction between arginine/serine-rich zinc knuckle-containing protein 32 (RS2Z32) splicing isoforms and the Arabidopsis thaliana ortholog of human splicing factor SC35 (SC35) leads to the formation of distinct complexes, through which the recognition of splice sites within intron 3 of the transcription factor circadian clock associated 1 (CCA1) gene is regulated, ultimately resulting in an altered ratio of the CCA1 splice variants. Competitive binding of CCA1α and CCA1β to the flowering locus C (FLC) gene promoter can either promote or inhibit FLC transcription and flowering. This study elucidates the molecular mechanism by which RS2Z32 regulates FLC expression independently of its canonical splicing function, enhancing our understanding of transcriptional regulation mediated by splicing factors in plants.

papers.title: The MaPUB23-mediated degradation of the MaHSFB1-MaHDA2 counteracts high temperature-inhibited chlorophyll degradation in banana
papers.abstract: Abstract Banana fruits ripening at or above 30 °C soften but retain a green peel. Elucidating the mechanism underlying this high temperature-induced repression of chlorophyll catabolism would help to improve the marketability of bananas. Toward this end, we compared banana fruits ripened at 20 °C and 30 °C using transcriptome analysis, revealing several E3 ubiquitin ligases repressed in green fruits ripened at 30 °C. Among them, only the U-box type E3 ligase MaPUB23 promoted chlorophyll degradation when transiently overexpressed in tobacco leaves. MaPUB23 interacted with and targeted MaHSFB1 and MaHDA2 for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. MaHSFB1 specifically interacted with and recruited MaHDA2 to the promoters of chlorophyll catabolic genes (CCGs), transcriptionally repressed these genes via decreased histone acetylation, and inhibited chlorophyll degradation. However, high temperature attenuated the MaPUB23-mediated degradation of MaHSFB1 and MaHDA2, which enhanced the MaHSFB1–MaHDA2-mediated repression of CCGs. These results suggest that high temperature attenuates the MaPUB23-mediated proteasomal degradation of MaHSFB1–MaHDA2, leading to green ripening in banana fruit. This study thus illustrates a novel, dynamic regulatory module controlling the high temperature-induced repression of chlorophyll catabolism in banana fruits. Elucidating this mechanism provides a theoretical basis for strategies to manage temperature-induced fruit quality deterioration.

papers.title: Phosphorylation Alters the Condensation State of the Potato Transcription Factor bZIP18 to Enhance Plant Immunity
papers.abstract: Abstract Biomolecular condensates formed by transcription factors (TFs) via liquid-liquid phase separation enable precise spatiotemporal control of eukaryotic gene expression. Although phosphorylation is a well-established regulator of TF activity, its capacity to remodel condensate organization and transcriptional function in plant immunity remains largely undefined. Here, we report that pathogen-induced phosphorylation converts a pre-existing TF condensate into a dynamic transcriptional hub to enhance the immune response in potato. Upon infection by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans, the mitogen-activated protein kinase StMPK9 phosphorylates the TF StbZIP18 at the conserved residue threonine 337. This modification triggers rapid changes in the nuclear StbZIP18 condensates, transforming pre-existing condensates into numerous smaller assemblies. The phospho-null StbZIP18T337A mutant maintains its presence in low-activity condensates and compromises immunity, whereas the phospho-mimetic variant StbZIP18T337E constitutively forms active condensates and enhances resistance. The gene encoding the TF StMYB44 was identified as the direct downstream gene target of StbZIP18. TurboID-based proximity labeling revealed that both wild-type StbZIP18 and StbZIP18T337E, but not the phospho-null variant StbZIP18T337A, selectively interact with the transcriptional cofactor StMBF1c to form transcriptional activation hubs that drive defense gene expression, including StMYB44. Together, our findings establish that phosphorylation-directed condensate reprogramming operates as a tunable phase-separation switch, converting a low-activity assembly into a transcriptional amplifier. This study unveils a biophysical mechanism for signal amplification in plant immunity and provides insight into how post-translational modifications modulate transcriptional condensate function.
papers.affiliation: State Key Laboratory for Crop Stress Resistance and High-Efficiency Production, College of Horticulture, Northwest A&F University , Yangling, Shaanxi 712100 ,

papers.title: Plant Single-Cell Metabolomics and Metabolite Imaging: Current Advances and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Abstract Plants are multicellular systems composed of highly specialized cell types, whose distinct transcriptomes, proteomes, and metabolomes collectively shape growth, development, defense, and environmental adaptation. While single-cell transcriptomics has transformed our understanding of plant cellular heterogeneity, metabolites provide a direct and integrative readout of cellular biochemical activity and physiological state and can offer valuable insights into phenotype. They provide essential information that gene expression alone does not capture. Recent advances in mass spectrometry-based single-cell metabolomics (scMet) have enabled direct measurement of metabolic variation across individual cells and subcellular domains. In parallel, mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) has emerged as a powerful approach for mapping the spatial organization of metabolites within intact plant organs, offering new opportunities to connect chemical diversity with anatomy, cell identity, and biological functions. This review summarizes current technologies for plant single-cell sampling, scMet, and MSI for spatial metabolomics. It further highlights emerging efforts to illuminate the plant’s cellular and spatial dark metabolome through spectral libraries, computational metabolomics, and AI-assisted annotation. A long-term objective is to build quantitative, spatially resolved, and biologically interpretable plant signaling and metabolic networks at single-cell resolution.
papers.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of Mississippi , Oxford, Mississippi 38677 ,

papers.title: A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping
Maize genetic diversity is largely unstructured by human ethnolinguistic diversity in its center of origin
papers.abstract: Population structure and environmental features often capture major axes of genetic variation in many species. Yet the impacts of human activity often remain unquantified. For domesticated species that rely on human activity for survival and dispersal, human movements and cultural differences may play key roles patterning genetic diversity. Maize is a staple crop of enormous cultural importance to indigenous peoples of the Americas, but cannot survive or disperse without farmers. Using publicly available genotyping and passport data from approximately 2,000 traditional maize varieties, more than 500 whole genome sequences of humans from Mexico, and indigenous linguistic maps, we quantify anthropogenic effects on maize genetic diversity in the Americas. Maize shows very little overall structure, highlighting the effectiveness of indigenous farmers in moving and mixing maize populations. While principal components of maize diversity show meaningful correlations to human genetic diversity, our linear modeling suggests little additional impact of human population structure beyond shared geography. Though differences in maize diversity are often patterned by language locally, we find only weak genome-wide effects at larger spatial scales. Despite the relatively weak global signal of anthropogenic effects, linguistic Genome-wide association, outlier F ST analyses, and selection scans identified loci associated with specific languages. Leveraging landscape-level sequencing data, we highlight how anthropogenic factors have shaped patterns of maize genetic diversity across Mesoamerica.

papers.title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root
papers.abstract: Abstract Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

papers.title: Core effectors of the Fusarium pan-effectome contribute to host specificity
papers.abstract: Fusarium fungi cause economically important diseases of cereal crops, including Fusarium head blight, ear blight, and root rot. Central to these interactions are secreted effector proteins that manipulate host biology to promote infection. In turn, plants have evolved to recognize effector activity to activate immune responses and restrict disease. Despite their importance, the diversity, conservation, and evolution of Fusarium effectors remain poorly understood. Here, we present the Fusarium sambucinum Species complex Effector Compendium (FUSEC), a sequence-defined pan-effectome constructed from 188 high-quality genomes representing 27 species. FUSEC comprises 4,057 sequence-defined effector families, including a conserved soft-core repertoire of 235 families present in at least 95% of isolates. Structure-guided comparisons reorganized these conserved families into 184 structure-defined groups, revealing relationships that extend beyond sequence similarity and identifying similarities to numerous experimentally characterized fungal (a)virulence factors. Despite their broad conservation, soft-core families exhibited substantial within-family sequence diversity, and analyses of diversifying selection identified 44 candidate families undergoing adaptive evolution. Functional screening revealed that the majority of these candidates altered wheat immune responses, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletions in Fusarium graminearum demonstrated that multiple conserved effectors contribute to cultivar-dependent Fusarium head blight severity.
papers.affiliation: Department of Cell and Systems Biology, University of Toronto
